report.summary: Reviewed chunk 3 of 3 of daedalus/spine/ledger.py: methods recent_intents, intents_matching_payload, resolve_by_effect, intents_for_trace, events, _hydrate, close, and helper _row_to_intent. All claims verified against code.
risks: intents_matching_payload | medium | LIKE with ESCAPE '\' may have unexpected behavior on some SQLite versions; relies on correct escaping logic. | Test with special characters like % and _.
intents_for_trace | medium | Catches OperationalError broadly, could mask unrelated errors if 'no such column' substring present in error message. | Ensure error message parsing is robust.
_row_to_intent | low | Uses row.keys() which may be expensive for large result sets; alternative is to check column names from cursor description. | Performance test with many rows.

handoff.purpose: Provides query methods for intents and events, and helper function to construct Intent objects from database rows.

symbols.name: recent_intents
symbols.note: Returns list of Intent objects ordered by id DESC, with optional kind filter and limit.

symbols.name: intents_matching_payload
symbols.note: Returns Intent list where payload contains given key-value pairs, using LIKE with escaped characters.

symbols.name: resolve_by_effect
symbols.note: Returns all intents with given effect_key, ordered by id ascending.

symbols.name: intents_for_trace
symbols.note: Returns intents with given trace_id, handles missing column gracefully.

symbols.name: events
symbols.note: Returns list of IntentEvent for a given intent_id, ordered by id ascending.

symbols.name: _hydrate
symbols.note: Converts a sqlite3.Row to an Intent, using terminal event if available.

symbols.name: close
symbols.note: Closes the database connection, ignoring errors.

symbols.name: __exit__
symbols.note: Context manager exit, calls close and returns False.

symbols.name: _row_to_intent
symbols.note: Helper to construct Intent from a row and additional parameters.

claims.text: Newest first because every caller wants recency; ``limit`` is applied in SQL so a long-lived ledger does not have to be hydrated in full to answer "what happened lately".
claims.why: Code uses ORDER BY id DESC and LIMIT ? applied in SQL, so only limit rows are fetched and hydrated.

claims.text: A non-positive limit returns nothing, which is the truthful answer to "give me zero rows" and keeps a caller's arithmetic (``limit=n-1``) from silently meaning "all".
claims.why: Code: if limit is not None and int(limit) <= 0: return []

claims.text: The targeted alternative to ``recent_intents(limit=N)``. A row limit is a WINDOW, not a bound: with it, the oldest attempts silently fall out of memory and their tasks become selectable again, so a loop would slowly start repeating work it had already done -- the exact defect the memory exists to prevent, reintroduced by the thing meant to make it cheap. Asking for the specific values a caller cares about has no such edge.
claims.why: This claim discusses behavior of recent_intents and broader system design; not verifiable from this chunk alone.

claims.text: Matching is a substring test against the payload TEXT, which is exact here rather than approximate because every payload is written through ``canonical_json``: sorted keys, no whitespace, ``ensure_ascii``. So a recorded ``key``/``value`` pair always appears verbatim as ``"key":"value"``. LIKE metacharacters in either are escaped, so a value containing ``%`` matches only a literal ``%``.
claims.why: Code constructs fragment via canonical_json and escapes % and _ (and backslash) for LIKE. The claim about payload format is uncheckable but the escaping logic is verified.

claims.text: A LOOKUP, not a mutation: given a token found in the world, this answers "which intent claimed it" so the caller can close that intent. It returns a list because retries legitimately reuse a key, and collapsing them to one would hide an attempt.
claims.why: Code only executes SELECT, no mutation. Returns list of rows, not single item.

claims.text: THE JOIN. This is the ledger's half of "what did that run actually do" -- the other halves are the loop ledger's ``trace_id`` and the bridge records', and all three carry the same value so one grep spans them.
claims.why: Refers to other components not in this chunk.

claims.text: Returns ``[]`` rather than raising on a pre-v2 database that has no such column. That is the correct answer, not a swallowed error: a v1 file provably contains no traced rows, so "no intents under this trace" is true, and making a status reader crash on an old ledger would punish exactly the reader that most needs to keep working.
claims.why: Code catches sqlite3.OperationalError and returns [] if 'no such column' in error message.

claims.text: The full append-only transition history for one intent.
claims.why: Code selects all rows from intent_events for given intent_id, ordered by id, which is append-only.

claims.text: DEFENSIVE, and not merely belt-and-braces: a read_only ledger skips _migrate entirely (mode=ro cannot ALTER), so a reader opened against an un-migrated v1 file gets rows with no trace_id column at all. Asking the ROW what it has keeps that reader working instead of turning "this database is older than you" into an IndexError.
claims.why: Code checks 'trace_id' in row.keys() before accessing, so missing column yields None.

observations.what: intents_matching_payload uses LIKE with ESCAPE '\' clause; the escaping replaces backslash first, then percent and underscore. This is correct for SQLite's default escape character.
intents_for_trace catches OperationalError broadly; if error message contains 'no such column' as substring, it returns []. Could mask other errors with similar text.
_row_to_intent uses row.keys() to check for column existence; this is a method that returns all column names. For large result sets, this may be slightly inefficient, but acceptable.
The module uses sqlite3.Row access by column name; all queries use SELECT * which depends on column order. This is fine as long as schema is consistent.
